summary: A full, timed EST I English practice test: Literacy Test 1 (Writing and Language, 44 questions, 35 minutes) and Literacy Test 2 (Reading, 52 questions, 65 minutes), with an explanation for every answer.

blocks.text: This is a complete practice version of the two English parts of EST I: **Literacy Test 1 (Writing and Language)** and **Literacy Test 2 (Reading)**. Every passage and question was written for this site by Mohamed Abdelkriem. The test is modelled on the skills that the EST Literacy tests measure; it is not made of official EST questions, and the real test may present questions in a different way.

rows: Four essays with numbered, underlined parts. Fix grammar and punctuation, and improve transitions, order, wording and relevance.
Five long passages (fiction, history, science with a table, a pair of opinion texts, humanities). Answer questions about ideas, details, words, structure, evidence and data.

blocks.text: These figures are as published by schools; check the latest official EST candidate guide on est.moe.gov.eg before your test.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone, no dictionary and no help, exactly as in the real test.
Do the two sections in one sitting if you can. The timer starts when you begin each section and the section ends when the time is up.
Work through the questions in order. You can mark a question and come back to it while the section is still open, but once a section ends you cannot return to it, just as in the real test.
Answer every question. A blank is always wrong; a careful guess may be right.

Each passage is repeated above each of its questions. In Literacy Test 1, only the part that question asks about is underlined and numbered. In Literacy Test 2, the paragraphs are numbered [1], [2], [3] so that questions can point to them.
At the end you see a practice percentage for each section. It is not an official EST scaled score; use it to measure your progress from one practice test to the next.

questions.p:
**Reading the River**
For thousands of years, the life of Egypt depended on a single yearly event: the summer flood of the Nile. When the river rose, it spread water and rich, dark silt across the fields. A good flood meant a full harvest__[1]; a weak one__ could mean hunger. Too much water was dangerous as well, because a very high flood could sweep away villages and ruin stored grain. Because so much depended on the water, rulers wanted to know exactly how high the river has risen each year.
Their solution was the nilometer, a structure built to measure the level of the river. One famous example still stands at the southern tip of Roda Island in Cairo. Built in the ninth century, visitors can still see a tall stone column inside it standing in a deep pit. A narrow stone staircase winds down the walls of the pit to the bottom, where the column begins. Tunnels link the pit to the Nile. When the river outside rose. Water flowed in and climbed the column, which was marked with careful measurements. Officials read these marks carefully and attentively with great care every day during the flood season.
The readings mattered for more than farming. Nevertheless, taxes were based on the height of the flood. When the water reached a high mark, officials expected a large harvest and collected more from farmers. When the water stayed low, they reduced their demands. The system was not perfect, but it allowed the state to plan ahead, since officials could estimate months in advance how much grain the country would produce.
In this way, a simple stone column became one of the most important tool's in the country's economy. Today, the Nile no longer floods each summer, because the Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970 controls the river's flow. Visitors can still walk down the stairs and stand beside the column that once decided whether a village would eat well or go hungry. The nilometer is no longer needed for its original purpose, but it still attracts visitors who want to see how earlier Egyptians sized up their river.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined part.
c: NO CHANGE
, and, a weak one
, a weak one
a weak one
questions.e: Both sides are complete sentences that are closely related, so a semicolon joins them correctly. A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and the comma after "and" is not needed.

questions.p:
**Forests at the Edge of the Sea**
Along parts of Egypt's Red Sea coast, small groups of trees grow in a place where few plants could survive: the salty, shallow water at the edge of the sea. Seen from a boat, they look like a low green wall rising straight out of the waves. These are mangroves, and the species found most often in the region is the grey mangrove. The ability of these trees to live in seawater __[12] make__ them unusual among plants.
Salt is usually deadly to plants, because it pulls water out of their cells. The grey mangrove deals with this problem in two ways. First, its roots filter out much of the salt before water enters the plant. Despite this, special glands on its leaves push out the salt that gets through. On a sunny day, tiny white crystals can sometimes be seen shining on the leaves.
Mangroves face a second challenge: the mud they grow in contains very little oxygen. To solve this, the grey mangrove sends up hundreds of thin, pencil-like roots that stick out of the mud. These roots, called pneumatophores, take in air when the tide is low. The roots also trap mud and fallen leaves, slowly building up the shore.
These unusual trees are valuable to the whole coast. Their tangled roots shelter young fish and shrimp, they also slow down waves that would otherwise wash the beach away. Some of the young fish that grow up among the roots may later move out to the coral reefs offshore. Herons and other birds build nests in the branches, constructing their homes there. Grey mangrove leaves are oval and pale grey underneath. In addition, leaves that fall into the water feed tiny animals at the base of the food chain.
Unfortunately, these forests are under pressure. Coastal building has cleared some areas, and pollution damages others. Similarly, several stretches of the coast have been declared protected areas. In these places, the mangroves which have stood for many years, can continue to shelter the creatures that depend on them. Elsewhere, volunteers have planted young mangroves in places where the old forests were lost. With such protection, trees that grow where few plants could survive may last for many more generations.
questions.q: [12] Choose the best version of the underlined part.
c: NO CHANGE
have made
are making
makes
questions.e: The subject is "The ability" (singular), not "trees", which is inside the phrase "of these trees". A singular subject takes "makes". The other choices are plural verbs.

Seen from a boat, they look like a low green wall rising straight out of the waves. These are mangroves, and the species found most often in the region is the grey mangrove. **The Radio on the Shelf**
For as long as I can remember, an old wooden radio sat on a shelf in my grandfather's flat in Tanta. To me it was simply part of the furniture, like the faded carpet and the calendar from a bank that no longer existed. It had not made a sound in years, but __[23] he refuses__ to throw it away. Whenever I asked him why, he would only smile and say that it was waiting for the right person.
Last summer, I decided that I might be that person. I had recently joined my school's electronics club, where I learned to use a soldering iron and read simple circuit diagrams. I spent my first evening reading about old radios, trying to understand what each part was meant to do. My grandfather agreed to let me try, on one condition: I had to explain every step to him as I worked.
Opening the back of the radio, a cloud of dust made me cough. Inside, the parts looked nothing like the neat diagrams in my club's workbook. Wires of faded colours ran in every direction, and several glass valves, which looked like small light bulbs, were covered in grime. I cleaned each part, checked each wire and I was testing the fuse.
I tested everything twice without finding a fault. For example, I noticed a single wire that had snapped where it joined the speaker. I soldered it back in place, plugged in the radio and turned the dial. At first there was only a soft hiss. Then, faintly, a man's voice popped up, reading the evening news.
My grandfather did not say anything for a long moment. Then he told me that he had bought the radio in 1967 with his first salary and had listened to football matches on it together with his brothers, all of them together. On match nights, he said, half the street used to crowd into the flat to listen.
The radio sits on the same shelf today, but it is no longer silent. Every Friday evening, him and I listen to it together. Sometimes we hear a match; sometimes we hear only the news.

questions.e: The story is told in the past ("sat", "had not made", "asked"), so the past tense "refused" keeps the verbs consistent. The other choices shift to the present or future.

questions.p:
**First Aid Belongs in Every School**
Imagine that a classmate suddenly collapses in the school playground. In the minutes before an ambulance arrives, the people nearby __[34] is__ the only help available. In such a moment, knowing what to do can make the difference between a frightening story and a tragic one. Yet most teenagers would not know what to do. For this reason, I believe that every secondary school should teach basic first aid as part of its regular timetable.
The first argument for first aid lessons is simple: in many emergencies, the first few minutes matter most. A person who is choking or bleeding heavily may not survive a long wait. Someone trained in simple techniques, such as clearing a blocked airway or pressing firmly on a wound, can keep the victim alive until professional help arrives. The trained person does not replace the doctor; he or she simply keeps the patient alive long enough for the doctor to help. Doctors often point out that these skills are not rocket science, even for young students.
Second, first aid training builds confidence. Students who have practised on training dummies are less likely to panic in a real emergency. They are also more likely to step forward instead of waiting for someone else to act. Training teaches them to think in a calm order: check that the area is safe, call for help and then act.
Some people argue that the school timetable is already too full. Therefore, first aid does not have to replace any existing subject. A few hours each term would be enough, and this amount of time would be sufficient to teach the most important skills. Local hospitals and charities, often willing to send trainers free of charge.
Finally, first aid is a skill that lasts a lifetime. Years after leaving school, a former student might use what she learned to help a neighbours child, a colleague at work or a stranger on the road. Few school subjects can have such a direct affect on other people's lives. First aid kits should be checked regularly to make sure nothing is missing.

**Passage 1 (Literary fiction).** This passage is adapted from an original short story. Yusuf is an apprentice in a clockmaker's shop in Alexandria in the early twentieth century.
**The Clockmaker's Apprentice**
[1] The shop of Hakim the clockmaker stood at the narrow end of a street that sloped down towards the harbour, and on windy afternoons the smell of salt crept in beneath its door and settled among the clocks. There were forty of them at least, hanging from the walls, standing upon the counter, crowding the shelves like an audience that had come early to a play. Yusuf had counted them on his first morning, three years before, and had never since troubled to count them again; he had learned instead to know them by their voices.
[2] For each clock had a voice. The tall walnut clock beside the door spoke slowly and with great dignity, as a judge might; the little brass carriage clocks chattered over one another like sparrows; and the French clock with the painted face, which no customer had ever offered to buy, gave a thin, apologetic chime a full second after all the others, as though it had only just remembered what it was meant to say. Yusuf, who was fourteen and not given to fancies, would have denied that he thought of them as people. Yet he never wound the French clock without murmuring to it, and he never passed the walnut clock without a small, involuntary straightening of the shoulders.
[3] His master was a man of few words and fewer smiles. He worked at a bench by the window, a glass screwed into one eye, and when he spoke at all it was usually to say "Again," and to push back across the bench whatever Yusuf had just presented to him. A wheel filed a hair too thin, a spring set a fraction out of true, a screw tightened with more force than it required: each came back with the same word. In his first year Yusuf had wept over that word in private. In his second he had hated it. By the third he had begun, without quite noticing, to say it to himself before his master could.
[4] It was on a grey afternoon in late autumn that the merchant came in. He was a large man in a coat too warm for the weather, and he set upon the counter a gold pocket watch that had plainly cost more than the whole shop. "It stopped last night," he said, "and I sail for Marseilles on Thursday. Can it be mended by then?"
[5] Hakim turned the watch over once in his fingers, opened its back, looked, and closed it again. Then, to Yusuf's astonishment, he held it out to his apprentice. "The boy will do it," he said.
[6] The merchant looked at Yusuf, and Yusuf looked at the floor. He was aware of a great many things at once: the heat in his face, the forty clocks ticking as if they too were waiting for an answer, the cold weight of the watch now lying in his palm. He was aware, above all, that his master had not looked at him while speaking, but had already turned back to his own bench, as a man turns from a question that has been settled.
[7] He worked on the watch for two days. He did not hurry, for hurrying was the surest way to hear "Again"; but neither did he linger, for Thursday was fixed and would not move for him. When at last he found the fault (a single tooth broken from the smallest wheel, so small that he had passed over it twice), he made a new wheel himself, filing it by lamplight long after the street outside had fallen silent.
[8] On Wednesday evening he laid the watch on his master's bench. Hakim lifted it, listened, and set it down. For a long moment he said nothing at all. Then he took up his own work again and remarked, without raising his eyes, "The French clock is slow. See to it before you go."
[9] Yusuf crossed to the French clock and opened its case. Behind him, all forty clocks began to strike seven, and for once the painted one struck with them.
questions.q: Which choice best summarises the passage?
c: An apprentice who has long been corrected by a demanding master is trusted with an important repair and completes it successfully.
A clockmaker teaches his apprentice how to deal politely with wealthy customers.
A merchant's urgent request causes a quarrel between a clockmaker and his apprentice.
A boy who dislikes his strict master decides to leave the shop after finishing one last job.
questions.e: The story moves from Hakim's constant "Again" to Yusuf repairing the merchant's watch alone and having it accepted. There is no lesson about customers, no plan to leave and no quarrel.

**Passage 2 (History and social studies).** This passage is adapted from an original article about the history of standard time.
**How the Railways Changed Time**
[1] For most of human history, time was a local matter. Each town set its clocks by the sun: when the sun stood highest in the sky, it was noon. Because the earth turns from west to east, noon arrives a little later for every step a traveller takes towards the west. A town a short ride to the west of its neighbour therefore kept a slightly different time, and nobody minded. A difference of a few minutes meant nothing to a farmer, and a traveller on horseback moved too slowly to notice it.
[2] The railway changed this. By the 1840s, trains in Britain could carry passengers across the country in hours rather than days, and the patchwork of local times suddenly became a serious problem. Bristol, in the west of England, kept time about ten minutes behind London. A timetable that listed departures in local time at every station was confusing for passengers and dangerous for railway workers, who needed to know exactly where each train was on a single track. One railway company after another solved the problem in the same way: it ran its trains on London time, set by the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, and sent the correct time along the line by telegraph.
[3] At first, this "railway time" existed alongside local time rather than replacing it. Some towns resisted. For people who had always lived by the sun, being told that noon now arrived when a distant observatory said so seemed an insult to common sense, and perhaps to local pride as well. In Bristol, a public clock was given two minute hands, one showing local time and one showing London time: a compromise that let citizens see both the old world and the new on a single face. Yet the practical advantages were difficult to argue with. By the time Parliament made Greenwich time the legal time for the whole of Great Britain in 1880, most of the country had long since adopted it in daily life.
[4] The problem was far larger in the United States, which stretches across a whole continent. American railroads ran on dozens of different local times, and a large station might display several clocks, each showing the time of a different railroad. On 18 November 1883, the railroads took matters into their own hands. They divided the country into standard time zones, and on that day clocks across the nation were reset. Some cities experienced what newspapers called "the day of two noons", as their clocks reached twelve, were turned back, and reached twelve again. Remarkably, this change was organised by private companies rather than by the government; the system did not become federal law until 1918.
[5] A year after the American change, delegates from around the world met in Washington, D.C., for the International Meridian Conference. They agreed that the line of longitude passing through Greenwich would serve as the starting point, the prime meridian, from which the world's longitude would be measured. Over the following decades, more and more countries organised their clocks into zones measured from Greenwich, though some took many years to do so.
[6] It is easy to forget how strange this transformation once seemed. We now accept without question that the time on our phones is set by agreement, not by the sun overhead. But that agreement was not inevitable. It was built, piece by piece, by engineers who needed trains to run safely, by companies seeking order, and by governments that eventually followed where the railways had led. In a real sense, the modern idea of time arrived on the same tracks as the trains.
questions.q: The passage is mainly concerned with
c: how the needs of the railways led to local solar time being replaced by standard time.
the role of the telegraph in the growth of the railways.
the scientific reasons why noon arrives later in western towns.
why Bristol refused to accept London time for many years.
questions.e: The passage follows the change from local sun time to railway time, time zones and the prime meridian. Bristol, the earth's rotation and the telegraph are details inside that larger story.

**Passage 3 (Science).** This passage is adapted from an original article about birdsong in cities. The study described is fictional, and its data are for practice only.
**Singing Over the Noise**
[1] Anyone who has stood beside a busy road knows how hard it can be to hold a conversation. Most of us respond in the same way: we raise our voices, and often, without realising it, we raise their pitch as well. Over the past few decades, biologists have found that many songbirds living in cities seem to do something similar. Their songs, compared with those of the same species in quiet forests, are often pitched higher.
[2] The reason seems to lie in the nature of traffic noise. The roar of engines and tyres is concentrated at low frequencies: deep sounds, the kind that rumble rather than whistle. A bird whose song includes low notes may find those notes drowned out, much as a quiet bass line disappears beneath the noise of a crowd. Higher notes, by contrast, stand out more clearly against the background. A bird that shifts its song upward, then, may be heard by rivals and possible mates that would otherwise miss it.
[3] To examine this idea in one species, a team led by ecologist Laila Mansour recorded the songs of great tits at four sites that differed sharply in noise. The quietest was a forest reserve far from any main road; the noisiest was a strip of trees beside a six-lane highway. At each site, the researchers measured the average level of background noise and recorded dozens of males singing during the spring breeding season. They then analysed each recording for the lowest note in the song and for the song's overall length. Their results are shown in the table.
Table: Background noise and great tit song at four sites
Site | Background noise (decibels) | Lowest note in song (kilohertz) | Average song length (seconds)
Forest reserve | 42 | 2.9 | 3.1
Suburban park | 55 | 3.3 | 2.8
City-centre park | 68 | 3.8 | 2.6
Roadside trees | 74 | 4.0 | 2.5
[4] The pattern was clear. As background noise increased from one site to the next, the lowest note in the birds' songs rose with it. Song length moved in the opposite direction: the noisiest sites had the shortest songs. Mansour suggests that shorter songs may be another way of coping with noise, although she admits that this explanation is less certain. "With pitch, we have a clear mechanism," she says. "With length, we have a pattern we cannot yet fully explain."
[5] The study also raised a question that recordings alone cannot answer. Are city birds adjusting their songs from moment to moment, the way a person raises their voice in a noisy café? Or have city populations, over many generations, come to sing differently in a more permanent way? To begin to separate these possibilities, the team returned to the city-centre park on several Friday mornings, when traffic was unusually light. On those mornings, many birds sang slightly lower notes than they did on working days. This suggests that at least part of the change is flexible, a response to the noise of the moment rather than a fixed trait.
[6] Higher songs may not be a costless solution. In many songbirds, females appear to prefer males that sing lower notes, perhaps because low notes are harder to produce and so signal a larger or healthier singer. questions.p:
**Passage 4 (Paired texts).** Text 1 and Text 2 are original opinion pieces about what cities should do with their old buildings.
**Text 1**
[1] When an old building is demolished, a city loses more than bricks and stone. It loses a record of how people once lived and worked, written in the shape of windows, the height of ceilings and the patterns of decoration that no modern builder would think to reproduce. A street of old houses is a kind of book that can be read only by walking through it, and once a page is torn out, it cannot be printed again. Old buildings also tell newcomers that a city has a memory, that it did not appear overnight.
[2] Defenders of demolition often argue that old buildings are inefficient, and it is true that many are draughty, badly lit and expensive to maintain. But these problems can usually be solved. Insulation can be added, wiring replaced and interiors adapted for new uses, as has been done with countless former factories, warehouses and railway stations around the world. Restoration is sometimes more expensive than building anew, but the cost of losing a city's character is one that no budget records.
[3] We should also remember that the most "efficient" choice is not always the one that looks cheapest. Constructing a new building uses enormous quantities of concrete, steel and energy. A sound old building that is repaired and reused has already paid much of that environmental cost. Every time we knock down a solid building, we throw away that investment and pay for it all over again. Preservation, in other words, is not merely an act of nostalgia. It is often the more responsible choice.
**Text 2**
[1] Few people want to live in a city without history. But a city is not a museum, and its first duty is to the people who live in it now. In many growing cities, families struggle to find homes they can afford, while protected old buildings occupy land that could house many times as many people. Young people in particular may be forced to move to distant suburbs, far from their work and their families. When every building over a certain age is treated as untouchable, the result can be a city that is beautiful to visit but impossible to live in.
[2] This does not mean that nothing old should survive. Buildings of genuine historical or artistic importance deserve protection, and the best of them should be restored with care. The difficulty lies in deciding which buildings meet that standard. Age alone is a poor guide: a building is not valuable simply because it is old, any more than it is worthless simply because it is new.
[3] Instead of protecting whole districts unchanged, cities should make careful choices. They might preserve the most significant buildings, allow others to be adapted, and permit new construction where the need for housing is greatest. Such an approach accepts that every generation adds its own layer to a city. Old and new can stand side by side, as they have in successful cities for centuries. The buildings we put up today, after all, may one day be the historic buildings that a future generation fights to save.
questions.q: The author of Text 1 mainly argues that
c: new buildings should be designed to copy the decoration of old ones.
old buildings are too expensive to repair and should be replaced.
old buildings should be preserved because they record the past and reusing them is often the responsible choice.
only buildings of artistic importance deserve protection.
questions.e: Text 1 praises old buildings as "a record of how people once lived" and calls preservation "the more responsible choice". Replacing them is the opposite view, protecting only important buildings is Text 2's position, and copying decoration is never suggested.

**Passage 4 (Paired texts).** Text 1 and Text 2 are original opinion pieces about what cities should do with their old buildings.
**Text 1**
[1] When an old building is demolished, a city loses more than bricks and stone. It loses a record of how people once lived and worked, written in the shape of windows, the height of ceilings and the patterns of decoration that no modern builder would think to reproduce. A street of old houses is a kind of book that can be read only by walking through it, and once a page is torn out, it cannot be printed again. Old buildings also tell newcomers that a city has a memory, that it did not appear overnight.
[2] Defenders of demolition often argue that old buildings are inefficient, and it is true that many are draughty, badly lit and expensive to maintain. But these problems can usually be solved. Insulation can be added, wiring replaced and interiors adapted for new uses, as has been done with countless former factories, warehouses and railway stations around the world. Restoration is sometimes more expensive than building anew, but the cost of losing a city's character is one that no budget records.
[3] We should also remember that the most "efficient" choice is not always the one that looks cheapest. Constructing a new building uses enormous quantities of concrete, steel and energy. A sound old building that is repaired and reused has already paid much of that environmental cost. Every time we knock down a solid building, we throw away that investment and pay for it all over again. Preservation, in other words, is not merely an act of nostalgia. It is often the more responsible choice.
**Text 2**
[1] Few people want to live in a city without history. But a city is not a museum, and its first duty is to the people who live in it now. In many growing cities, families struggle to find homes they can afford, while protected old buildings occupy land that could house many times as many people. Young people in particular may be forced to move to distant suburbs, far from their work and their families. When every building over a certain age is treated as untouchable, the result can be a city that is beautiful to visit but impossible to live in.
[2] This does not mean that nothing old should survive. Buildings of genuine historical or artistic importance deserve protection, and the best of them should be restored with care. The difficulty lies in deciding which buildings meet that standard. Age alone is a poor guide: a building is not valuable simply because it is old, any more than it is worthless simply because it is new.
[3] Instead of protecting whole districts unchanged, cities should make careful choices. They might preserve the most significant buildings, allow others to be adapted, and permit new construction where the need for housing is greatest. Such an approach accepts that every generation adds its own layer to a city. Old and new can stand side by side, as they have in successful cities for centuries. The buildings we put up today, after all, may one day be the historic buildings that a future generation fights to save.
questions.q: On which point would the authors of both texts most likely agree?
c: Some old buildings are worth preserving and restoring with care.
The need for affordable housing matters more than history.
Restoring old buildings is always cheaper than replacing them.
Every building over a certain age should be protected.
questions.e: Text 1 defends preserving old buildings, and Text 2 agrees that buildings of real importance "deserve protection" and should be "restored with care". Text 2 rejects protecting everything old, Text 1 does not rank housing above history, and neither says restoration is always cheaper.

**Passage 5 (Humanities).** This passage is adapted from an original essay about the art of translation.
**The Invisible Art**
[1] When we praise a novel written in another language, we rarely mention the person whose words we actually read. A reader may finish a translated book, recommend it to friends and quote its finest sentences, all without noticing the translator's name in small print on the title page. Reviews of translated novels often praise the author's beautiful style without asking whose style the reader has actually been enjoying. For many translators, this invisibility is a sign of success. A good translation, an old saying goes, should read as though it had been written in the reader's own language.
[2] Yet the ideal of the invisible translator hides how much a translator must decide. Languages do not divide the world in the same way. Arabic distinguishes between a father's brother, "amm", and a mother's brother, "khal", where English offers only "uncle". A translator working from Arabic into English must choose whether to keep the distinction, explain it, or quietly let it disappear. Each choice gains something and loses something, and none of them is neutral. Even a word as simple as "you" can cause trouble, since many languages, Arabic among them, use different forms for a man and a woman.
[3] The difficulty grows with humour, poetry and wordplay. A joke that depends on two meanings of a single word may have no equivalent at all in another language. Poetry is harder still, because a poem's meaning lives not only in its words but in its sounds, rhythms and rhymes. A translator who keeps the exact meaning of each line may lose the music that made the poem memorable; one who keeps the music may have to change what the lines say. Some translators have compared the task to playing a piece written for the piano on a violin: the melody can survive, but it will never sound quite the same.
[4] For this reason, some writers argue that translators should become more visible, not less. They suggest that translations might include short notes explaining difficult choices, or that the translator's name should appear on the cover beside the author's. Readers, in this view, deserve to know that they are reading one person's interpretation of another's work. Others reply that notes and explanations interrupt the experience of reading and remind us constantly that something has been lost. A novel, they say, should be enjoyed as a novel, not studied as a puzzle.
[5] Both sides, however, agree on a basic point: translation is a creative act. It requires the translator to understand not just the words of the original but its tone, its humour and its historical setting, and then to rebuild all of these in a language with different tools. In this sense, a translator is less like a photocopier than like an architect asked to rebuild a house in a city where none of the original materials can be found.
[6] Perhaps the most useful way to think of a translation, then, is neither as a perfect copy nor as a poor imitation, but as a conversation between two languages. Something is always lost in that conversation. But something is also found: new expressions, new ways of seeing, and, for readers who could never have read the original, a door into a world that would otherwise have remained closed. The next time you finish a translated book, it may be worth turning back to the title page to find out whose voice you have been listening to.

c: poetry should never be translated because its music is always lost.
translation involves many difficult, creative choices and is far more than invisible copying.

A reader may finish a translated book, recommend it to friends and quote its finest sentences, all without noticing the translator's name in small print on the title page. Reviews of translated novels often praise the author's beautiful style without asking whose style the reader has actually been enjoying. For many translators, this invisibility is a sign of success. A good translation, an old saying goes, should read as though it had been written in the reader's own language.
[2] Yet the ideal of the invisible translator hides how much a translator must decide. Languages do not divide the world in the same way. Arabic distinguishes between a father's brother, "amm", and a mother's brother, "khal", where English offers only "uncle". A translator working from Arabic into English must choose whether to keep the distinction, explain it, or quietly let it disappear. Each choice gains something and loses something, and none of them is neutral. Even a word as simple as "you" can cause trouble, since many languages, Arabic among them, use different forms for a man and a woman.
[3] The difficulty grows with humour, poetry and wordplay. A joke that depends on two meanings of a single word may have no equivalent at all in another language. Poetry is harder still, because a poem's meaning lives not only in its words but in its sounds, rhythms and rhymes. A translator who keeps the exact meaning of each line may lose the music that made the poem memorable; one who keeps the music may have to change what the lines say. Some translators have compared the task to playing a piece written for the piano on a violin: the melody can survive, but it will never sound quite the same.
[4] For this reason, some writers argue that translators should become more visible, not less. They suggest that translations might include short notes explaining difficult choices, or that the translator's name should appear on the cover beside the author's. Readers, in this view, deserve to know that they are reading one person's interpretation of another's work. Others reply that notes and explanations interrupt the experience of reading and remind us constantly that something has been lost. A novel, they say, should be enjoyed as a novel, not studied as a puzzle.

It requires the translator to understand not just the words of the original but its tone, its humour and its historical setting, and then to rebuild all of these in a language with different tools. In this sense, a translator is less like a photocopier than like an architect asked to rebuild a house in a city where none of the original materials can be found.

questions.q: The comparison of a translator to an architect in paragraph [5] suggests that a translator must
c: recreate the original work using different resources rather than simply copy it.
travel to the country where the original was written.
use only the words that appear in the original text.

questions.q: Which choice best describes the author's view of translation in the final paragraph?
c: Balanced but positive: something is always lost, yet translation also gives readers something valuable.
Entirely negative: translation always produces a poor imitation.
Unrealistic: the author claims that a perfect translation is possible.
Uncertain: the author cannot decide whether translation is useful.
questions.e: The author admits "Something is always lost" but stresses that "something is also found", including "a door into a world". The paragraph rejects both "perfect copy" and "poor imitation" and ends on a clear, positive note.

items: Read the explanation for every question, including the ones you got right; a lucky guess is not a skill yet.
Write down the skill tag of every question you missed (for example Punctuation, Transitions, Inference or Data and graphics) and count which tags appear most often. Those are your weak skills.

For Literacy Test 1 mistakes, go back to "EST Literacy Test 1: Writing and Language" and open the lesson for each weak skill from its table "Where each skill is fully taught on this site" (for example Sentence Boundaries, Commas and Extra Information, Transitions, Concision and Redundancy, Relevance: Add, Delete and Writer's Goal, Organisation: Order and Transitions, Word Choice and Tone).

For Literacy Test 2 mistakes, go back to "EST Literacy Test 2: Reading" and its lesson table (for example Central Ideas and Details, Inferences, Words in Context, Text Structure and Purpose, Command of Evidence: Textual, Command of Evidence: Quantitative, Cross-Text Connections).

If you ran out of time, reread the pacing plans on the two guide pages and "The EST Explained", then retake this test with the timer on, or try a Digital SAT or ACT practice test on this site for extra timed practice.
